catalog_quote: [2025 abstract:] "Awiakay has twelve consonants and twelve vowels, primary stress occurs on the first syllable." [2015 thesis, App. A sec. 1.1.3, pp. 290-291:] "Each diphthong is a single syllable and carries a single stress. In contrast to diphthongs, true vowel sequences always belong to two syllables and each vowel carries separate stress. ... The minimal pair [wái] 'stomach, belly' : [wá·ì·] 'wind'; 'string bag' (TP bilum) proves that there is a phonemic contrast between the diphthong /aɪ/ and the vowel sequence /ai/. [wái] <way> 'stomach', 'belly' is a monosyllabic word, while [wá·ì·] <wai> 'wind'; 'string bag' has two syllables, the first one carrying the primary, the second one the secondary stress."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of the word (per the author's chapter abstract); the thesis example wa.i 'wind' shows primary stress on syllable 1 and secondary on syllable 2, consistent with initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Thesis example gives secondary stress on the second syllable of a disyllable (wa.i); no general secondary-stress rule seen.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement; abstract says 'primary stress occurs on the first syllable' without specifying morphological domain or phrase effects.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Awiakay as spoken in Kanjimei village (c. 300-400 speakers), i.e. the Awiakay half of Glottolog's Awiakay-Karimba (awia1234); Karimba is not separately described.

In contrast to diphthongs, true vowel sequences always belong to two syllables and each vowel carries separate stress.' and the example [wa.i] <wai> 'wind; string bag' 'has two syllables, the first one carrying the primary, the second one the secondary stress' (pp. 290-291). a full-text search for stress/accent finds no other stress statement.
